faqs.a: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Matrices represent transformations, systems of equations, and data tables. A 2x2 matrix has 2 rows and 2 columns.
Multiply each row of the first matrix by each column of the second and sum the products. For 2x2: C[1,1] = A[1,1]*B[1,1] + A[1,2]*B[2,1]. Order matters: A x B is usually not equal to B x A.
faqs.q: How do you multiply two matrices?

faqs.a: The determinant is a single number computed from a square matrix. For 2x2 [[a,b],[c,d]] it is ad - bc. A zero determinant means the matrix is singular - it has no inverse and squashes space flat.
The inverse A^-1 is the matrix that undoes A: A x A^-1 = identity matrix. It exists only when the determinant is non-zero. You use it to solve matrix equations like A x = b via x = A^-1 b.

A singular matrix has determinant zero and no inverse. Geometrically it collapses space into fewer dimensions - for example, projecting 3D onto a plane. This calculator detects singular matrices and says so instead of producing garbage.

Yes - addition, subtraction and element-wise structure all work for any same-sized pair. Multiplication needs the inner dimensions to match. This tool fixes both matrices to the same square size, so everything lines up.

matrix-calculator.formula:
Addition: (A+B)[i,j] = A[i,j] + B[i,j]
Multiplication: (AB)[i,j] = sum over k of A[i,k] x B[k,j]
2x2 determinant: det = ad - bc
Inverse: A x A^-1 = I (exists only when det != 0)
howTo: Choose the operation: add, subtract, multiply, determinant or inverse.
Type the numbers into matrix A (and matrix B for two-matrix operations).
The result appears instantly below the inputs.
For inverse, check the determinant is non-zero - singular matrices are flagged.
keyFacts: A matrix is a grid of numbers with rows and columns; a 2x2 has 2 rows and 2 columns.
Addition and subtraction work entry by entry on same-sized matrices.
Multiplication combines rows of the first with columns of the second; order matters.
The 2x2 determinant is ad - bc for [[a,b],[c,d]].
An inverse exists only when the determinant is non-zero.
A x A^-1 equals the identity matrix (1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere).
